description_full: WD-40 Company engages in the provision of maintenance products, and homecare and cleaning products in North America, Central and South America, Asia, Australia, Europe, India, the Middle East, and Africa. The company offers multi-purpose maintenance products and specialty maintenance products, including WD-40 Multi-Use Product, an aerosol spray with various unique delivery systems, a non-aerosol trigger spray, a precision pen, and in liquid-bulk used for household, marine, automotive, construction, repair, sporting goods, and gardening applications; and WD-40 Specialist product line which includes penetrants, degreasers, corrosion inhibitors, greases, lubricants, and rust removers. It also provides multi-purpose drip and specialty oil lubricant; professional-grade aerosol specialty maintenance products, such as 3-IN-ONE RVcare products, 3-IN-ONE garage door lubricant, and 3-IN-ONE lock dry lube; and spray maintenance products and lubricants under the GT85 brand. In addition, the company offers automatic toilet bowl cleaners under the 2000 Flushes brand; aerosol and a liquid trigger carpet stain and odor eliminator under the Spot Shot brand; room and rug deodorizers sold as powder and aerosol quick-dry foam products under the Carpet Fresh brand; and heavy-duty hand cleaner, automatic toilet bowl cleaners, aerosol foaming carpet, fabric sanitizers, deodorizers, spot stain cleaners, and hand cleaner products under the Lava, X-14, no vac, and Solvol brands. It sells its products primarily through hardware stores, automotive parts outlets, industrial distributors and suppliers, mass retail and home center stores, value retailers, grocery stores, online retailers, warehouse club stores, farm supply stores, sport retailers, and independent bike dealers. WD-40 Company was founded in 1953 and is headquartered in San Diego, California.
ceo_bio: Mr. Steven A. Brass | CEO, President & Director | Age 59 | Compensation: $1.8M (FY2026)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 753 people. Revenue per employee of $914K ranks in the top quartile among Basic Materials peers, with revenue growing 5%/yr across its filed history. Each employee generates $130K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $10K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: WD-40 Company is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $3.0B market cap on $688M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +9% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 27% against a 8% cost of capital — a 19-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 54% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $98M in free cash flow — roughly 14 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.27× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.1× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 39× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 147% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Weakness in commodity prices pressures materials companies
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
35 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible

sect: Its 16% operating margin runs 7pp above the Basic Materials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.22x).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 221 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 25% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.64, it is more defensive than the market.
About $23.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 26% in the 2020 crash, 41% in the 2022 bear market and 43% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $90.45 (margin of safety -147%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 17%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $74.25 to $112 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 36.7 vs 16.3, EV/EBITDA 25.0 vs 8.3 and P/FCF 30.7 vs 22.4 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-3%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 3 covering analysts target $254 on average, 14% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 27% clears the cost of capital of 8.0% by 19pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.88).
It runs a 54% gross margin and converts 14% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.27x.
ROE of 30% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.2% of revenue on R&D and 1.1% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.1x net debt to EBITDA ($70.6M of cash against $86.0M of debt), with interest covered 39.3x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 12.3, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.6% over 3 years, 7.1% over 5 years and 6.1% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 7.0% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.1% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.9%), and institutions hold 91%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 2 sales over the past year.
It returns 2.8% a year to shareholders (1.0% in buybacks and 1.8% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 35 consecutive years, raising it 7.2% a year over the last five.
people: With about 753 employees, each generates about $914K of revenue, 1.4x the Basic Materials median, and revenue has grown 5.1% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $130K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.8M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
